paragraphs: The FOURTH class comprises the following miscellaneous powers:
1. A power "to promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries."

The usefulness of this power will scarcely be questioned. In Great Britain the copyright of authors has been solemnly judged to be a right of common law. The right to useful inventions seems, with equal reason, to belong to the inventors. In both cases the public good fully coincides with the claims of individuals. The States cannot separately make effective provision for either case, and most of them have anticipated the decision of this point by passing laws at the request of Congress.

2. "To exercise exclusive legislation, in all cases whatsoever, over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) as may, by cession of particular States and the acceptance of Congress, become the seat of the government of the United States; and to exercise like authority over all places purchased by the consent of the legislatures of the States in which the same shall be, for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings."

The indispensable necessity of complete authority at the seat of government carries its own evidence with it. Every legislature in the Union, I might say in the world, exercises this power by virtue of its general supremacy. Without it, public authority might be insulted and its proceedings interrupted with impunity. Worse, the members of the general government would depend for protection in the performance of their duty on the State that contains the seat of government, and this might bring on the national councils an imputation of awe or influence, equally dishonorable to the government and displeasing to the other members of the Confederacy. This consideration carries more weight because the gradual accumulation of public improvements at the permanent residence of the government would be too great a public pledge to leave in the hands of a single State, and would create so many obstacles to removing the government as to abridge still further its necessary independence. The extent of this federal district is limited enough to satisfy every jealousy of the opposite kind. And since the district is to be set aside for this use with the consent of the State ceding it; since the State will no doubt provide in the compact for the rights and the consent of the citizens living in it; since the inhabitants will find sufficient inducements of interest to become willing parties to the cession; since they will have had their voice in electing the government that is to exercise authority over them; since a municipal legislature for local purposes, derived from their own votes, will of course be allowed them; and since the authority of the State legislature, and of the inhabitants of the ceded part of the State, to concur in the cession will be derived from the whole people of the State in their adoption of the Constitution, every imaginable objection seems to be removed.

The necessity of a like authority over forts, magazines, etc., established by the general government is no less evident. The public money spent on such places, and the public property stored in them, require that they be exempt from the authority of the particular State. Nor would it be proper for the places on which the security of the entire Union may depend to be in any degree dependent on a particular member of it. All objections and scruples are removed here also by requiring the concurrence of the States concerned in every such establishment.
3. "To declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attained."

Since treason may be committed against the United States, the authority of the United States ought to be able to punish it. But new-fangled and artificial treasons have been the great engines by which violent factions, the natural offspring of free government, have usually vented their malignity on each other in turn. The Convention has therefore, with great judgment, set up a barrier against this peculiar danger. It has inserted a constitutional definition of the crime, fixed the proof necessary for conviction and restrained Congress, even in punishing treason, from extending the consequences of guilt beyond the person of its author.

4. "To admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent of the legislatures of the States concerned, as well as of the Congress."

The articles of Confederation contain no provision on this important subject. Canada was to be admitted of right on joining in the measures of the United States, and the other COLONIES, by which were evidently meant the other British colonies, at the discretion of nine States. The eventual establishment of NEW STATES seems to have been overlooked by the compilers of that instrument. We have seen the problem this omission caused, and the assumption of power into which it led Congress. The new system has therefore, with great propriety, supplied the defect. The general precaution that no new States shall be formed without the concurrence of the federal authority and of the States concerned is consistent with the principles that ought to govern such transactions. The particular precaution against creating new States by dividing a State without its consent quiets the jealousy of the larger States, as a like precaution against joining States without their consent quiets that of the smaller.

5. "To dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States," with a proviso that "nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State."

This is a power of very great importance, and it is required by considerations similar to those that show the propriety of the preceding one. The attached proviso is proper in itself, and was probably made absolutely necessary by jealousies and questions concerning the Western territory that are sufficiently known to the public.

6. "To guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; to protect each of them against invasion; and on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence."

In a confederacy founded on republican principles and composed of republican members, the superintending government clearly ought to have authority to defend the system against aristocratic or monarchical innovations. The more intimate the nature of such a union, the greater interest the members have in each other's political institutions, and the greater right they have to insist that the forms of government under which the compact was entered into be SUBSTANTIALLY maintained. But a right implies a remedy; and where else could the remedy be placed than where the Constitution places it? Governments of dissimilar principles and forms have been found less suited to a federal coalition of any sort than those of a kindred nature. "As the confederate republic of Germany," says Montesquieu, "consists of free cities and petty states, subject to different princes, experience shows us that it is more imperfect than that of Holland and Switzerland." "Greece was undone," he adds, "as soon as the king of Macedon obtained a seat among the Amphictyons." In the latter case, no doubt, the disproportionate force of the new member, as well as its monarchical form, had its share of influence on events. It may possibly be asked what need there could be for such a precaution, and whether it may not become a pretext for alterations in the State governments without the concurrence of the States themselves. These questions admit of ready answers. If the interposition of the general government should not be needed, the provision for such an event will be only a harmless superfluity in the Constitution. But who can say what experiments may be produced by the caprice of particular States, by the ambition of enterprising leaders or by the intrigues and influence of foreign powers? To the second question it may be answered that if the general government should interpose by virtue of this constitutional authority, it will of course be bound to pursue the authority. But the authority extends no further than to a GUARANTY of a republican form of government, which supposes a pre-existing government of the form that is to be guaranteed. As long, therefore, as the States continue their existing republican forms, the federal Constitution guarantees them. Whenever the States may choose to substitute other republican forms, they have a right to do so and to claim the federal guaranty for the latter. The only restriction imposed on them is that they shall not exchange republican for antirepublican Constitutions, a restriction that, it is presumed, will hardly be considered a grievance.

A protection against invasion is due from every society to the parts composing it. The breadth of the expression used here seems to secure each State not only against foreign hostility but against ambitious or vindictive enterprises of its more powerful neighbors. The history of both ancient and modern confederacies proves that the weaker members of a union ought not to be insensible to the policy of this article.

Protection against domestic violence is added with equal propriety. It has been remarked that even among the Swiss cantons, which, properly speaking, are not under one government, provision is made for this object. The history of that league tells us that mutual aid is frequently claimed and given, by the most democratic cantons as well as the others. A recent and well-known event among ourselves has warned us to be prepared for emergencies of a like nature.

At first view it might seem not to square with republican theory to suppose either that a majority lacks the right, or that a minority will have the force, to subvert a government; and consequently that federal interposition can never be required except when it would be improper. But theoretical reasoning, in this as in most other cases, must be qualified by the lessons of practice. Why may not illicit combinations for purposes of violence be formed by a majority of a State, especially a small State, as well as by a majority of a county or a district of the same State? And if the authority of the State ought, in the latter case, to protect the local magistracy, ought not the federal authority, in the former case, to support the State authority? Besides, there are certain parts of the State constitutions so interwoven with the federal Constitution that a violent blow cannot be struck at one without wounding the other. Insurrections in a State will rarely induce federal interposition unless the number involved in them bears some proportion to the friends of government. It will be much better for the violence in such cases to be repressed by the superintending power than for the majority to be left to maintain its cause by a bloody and obstinate contest. The existence of a right to interpose will generally prevent the necessity of exerting it.

Is it true that force and right are necessarily on the same side in republican governments? May not the minority party possess such a superiority of money, of military talent and experience, or of secret aid from foreign powers as will make it superior also in an appeal to the sword? May not a more compact and advantageous position turn the scale in its favor against a superior number so situated as to be less capable of a prompt and concentrated exertion of its strength? Nothing can be more fanciful than to imagine that in a trial of actual force victory may be calculated by the rules that prevail in a census of the inhabitants, or that determine the outcome of an election! May it not happen, in short, that the minority of CITIZENS may become a majority of PERSONS, by the addition of alien residents, of a chance crowd of adventurers, or of those whom the constitution of the State has not admitted to the rights of suffrage? I take no notice of an unhappy class of the population, abundant in some of the States, who during the calm of regular government are sunk below the level of men, but who in the stormy scenes of civil violence may emerge into the human character and give a superiority of strength to any party they may join.

In cases where it may be doubtful on which side justice lies, what better umpires could two violent factions, flying to arms and tearing a State to pieces, desire than the representatives of confederate States, not heated by the local flame? To the impartiality of judges they would unite the affection of friends. Happy would it be if all free governments could enjoy such a remedy for their infirmities, if an equally effective project could be established for the universal peace of mankind!

Should it be asked what the redress is to be for an insurrection that pervades all the States and commands a superiority of the entire force, though not a constitutional right, the answer must be this. Such a case, as it would be beyond the compass of human remedies, is fortunately not within the compass of human probability. And it is a sufficient recommendation of the federal Constitution that it diminishes the risk of a calamity for which no possible constitution can provide a cure.

Among the advantages of a confederate republic enumerated by Montesquieu, an important one is "that should a popular insurrection happen in one of the States, the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound."

7. "To consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation."

This can only be considered a declaratory proposition. It may have been inserted, among other reasons, for the satisfaction of the foreign creditors of the United States, who cannot be strangers to the pretended doctrine that a change in the political form of civil society has the magical effect of dissolving its moral obligations.

Among the lesser criticisms that have been leveled at the Constitution, it has been remarked that the validity of engagements ought to have been asserted in favor of the United States as well as against them. In the spirit that usually characterizes little critics, the omission has been turned into a plot against the national rights, and magnified. The authors of this discovery may be told what few others need to be told: that since engagements are by nature reciprocal, asserting their validity on one side necessarily involves their validity on the other; and that since the article is merely declaratory, establishing the principle in one case is sufficient for every case. They may be told further that every constitution must limit its precautions to dangers that are not altogether imaginary, and that no real danger can exist that the government would DARE, with or even without this constitutional declaration before it, to remit the debts justly due to the public on the pretext here condemned.
8. "To provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only."

That experience would suggest useful alterations could not but be foreseen. It was therefore necessary to provide a way of introducing them. The way the Convention preferred seems to be stamped with every mark of propriety. It guards equally against that extreme facility which would make the Constitution too changeable and that extreme difficulty which might perpetuate its discovered faults. It also equally enables the general and the State governments to originate the amendment of errors, as experience on one side or the other may point them out. The exception in favor of equality of suffrage in the Senate was probably meant as a palladium of the residuary sovereignty of the States, implied and secured by that principle of representation in one branch of the legislature, and was probably insisted on by the States particularly attached to that equality. The other exception must have been admitted on the same considerations that produced the privilege it defends.
9. "The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same."

This article speaks for itself. The express authority of the people alone could give due validity to the Constitution. To have required the unanimous ratification of the thirteen States would have subjected the essential interests of the whole to the caprice or corruption of a single member. It would have shown a lack of foresight in the Convention that our own experience would have made inexcusable.

Two questions of a very delicate nature present themselves on this occasion. 1. On what principle can the Confederation, which stands in the solemn form of a compact among the States, be superseded without the unanimous consent of the parties to it? 2. What relation is to exist between the nine or more States ratifying the Constitution and the remaining few that do not become parties to it?

The first question is answered at once by turning to the absolute necessity of the case; to the great principle of self-preservation; to the transcendent law of nature and of nature's God, which declares that the safety and happiness of society are the objects at which all political institutions aim, and to which all such institutions must be sacrificed. PERHAPS, also, an answer may be found without searching beyond the principles of the compact itself. It has been noted before, among the defects of the Confederation, that in many of the States it received no higher sanction than a mere legislative ratification. The principle of reciprocity seems to require that its obligation on the other States be reduced to the same standard. A compact between independent sovereigns, founded on ordinary acts of legislative authority, can claim no higher validity than a league or treaty between the parties. It is an established doctrine on the subject of treaties that all the articles are mutually conditions of each other; that a breach of any one article is a breach of the whole treaty; and that a breach committed by either of the parties absolves the others and authorizes them, if they please, to pronounce the compact violated and void. Should it unhappily be necessary to appeal to these delicate truths to justify dispensing with the consent of particular States to a dissolution of the federal pact, will not the complaining parties find it a difficult task to answer the MULTIPLIED and IMPORTANT infractions with which they may be confronted? There was a time when it was incumbent on us all to veil the ideas this paragraph presents. The scene is now changed, and with it the part that the same motives dictate.

The second question is no less delicate, and the flattering prospect that it will be merely hypothetical forbids an overcurious discussion of it. It is one of those cases that must be left to provide for itself. In general it may be observed that although no political relation can exist between the assenting and dissenting States, the moral relations will remain uncancelled. The claims of justice, on both sides, will be in force and must be fulfilled. The rights of humanity must in all cases be duly and mutually respected. And it is hoped that considerations of common interest, and above all the remembrance of the endearing scenes that are past and the anticipation of a speedy triumph over the obstacles to reunion, will not urge in vain MODERATION on one side and PRUDENCE on the other.
